Episode 41 of a daily journey through the universe. 📡
Season 3: the mysteries begins. In 1977 a radio telescope in Ohio caught a powerful signal from space that lasted 72 seconds and never came back. An astronomer circled it and wrote "Wow!". Was it aliens? A 2024 study offers a natural explanation.

segments.text: Episode forty-one. Season three: the mysteries. Next stop... the Wow signal.
On August fifteenth, nineteen seventy-seven, a radio telescope in Ohio called Big Ear was quietly scanning the sky.

visual.query: Big Ear radio observatory Ohio State
visual.commons: Big Ear radio observatory Ohio State

segments.headline: Big Ear, Ohio

segments.text: Suddenly it picked up a signal far stronger than the background noise of space.
Days later, astronomer Jerry Ehman was reading the computer printout. He circled the signal and wrote one word in the margin: Wow.
segments.headline: He wrote: Wow!

segments.text: The signal lasted seventy-two seconds. Exactly as long as the telescope took to sweep past one point in the sky.
It came near the frequency of hydrogen, the most common element in the universe. Scientists had suggested aliens might use that exact channel to say hello.
segments.headline: The hydrogen channel

segments.text: It seemed to come from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius.
segments.headline: Toward Sagittarius

segments.text: Astronomers have pointed telescopes at that spot again and again for nearly fifty years. The signal never returned.

In twenty twenty-four, a team using old data from the Arecibo telescope suggested a natural cause. A burst of energy, maybe from a dead star, may have made a cold hydrogen cloud flash brightly for a moment.
segments.headline: A natural explanation?

segments.text: But no one can prove it. The Wow signal is still one of the greatest mysteries of the radio sky.
